backups.name: Southeast Slopes
hazards: Off-trail bushwhacking through devil's club, vine maple, and blowdown between the Indian Creek Trail and Airplane Lake, worsened by sections of burned/dead forest
Stream crossings of the White River and Indian Creek that get noticeably harder in the afternoon as snowmelt raises water levels
Hidden cliff bands north of Airplane Lake that complicate the northeast ridge approach and can cliff out unwary parties
Lingering snow on the upper east face/slopes into July (continuous above ~4,700 ft in one logged July ascent), requiring an ice axe and step-kicking skills
Loose rock and steep talus on some summit approach variations
Sheer northwest face — not a descent or bail option
backups.overview: Mount Saul is the fourth-highest point on Wenatchee Ridge, a spur of the Cascade crest in the Glacier Peak Wilderness. It has a bare granitic summit with jagged rocks, a sheer northwest face, and a south side that drops nearly 4,000 ft to Indian Creek Valley in about a mile — the mountain punches well above its modest elevation for alpine character. There is no maintained trail to the top; climbers approach via the Indian Creek Trail from the White River drainage, then leave the trail near Airplane Creek for an off-trail scramble past Airplane Lake to the upper east slopes and summit rocks.
backups.beta: Southeast Slopes is Mount Saul's standard (and effectively only well-documented) route: a long approach with a short technical finish. From the White River Trailhead, follow Indian Creek Trail #1502 up the valley, then pick up an unofficial, unmarked path that climbs steeply past Airplane Lake to a saddle on the peak's southeast ridge, finishing with class 3 scrambling on rock that is solid in places and loose in others. It is typically done unroped, either as a very long day or as an overnight with a camp along Indian Creek.
backups.turnaround: Turn around before committing to the class 3 ridge if it is wet, snow-covered, or if afternoon thunderstorms are building, since the scramble and the long, faint cross-country approach are both harder to reverse safely in poor visibility or a storm.
backups.rappels: None normally needed; descend via the ascent route
backups.permit: Free self-issuing Glacier Peak Wilderness permit required, available at the White River Trailhead kiosk (confirmed via Okanogan-Wenatchee NF / White River Trailhead official page).
backups.descent: Reverse the ascent slopes to the approach drainage.

waypoints.name: White River / Indian Creek Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of White River Road/FS-6400 past Coles Corner; self-issue wilderness permit and a Northwest Forest Pass are required at the kiosk here.
waypoints.directions: From Leavenworth take US-2 west 15 miles to Coles Corner, turn onto SR-207 (Lake Wenatchee Highway) for 10.5 miles, then follow White River Road/FS-6400 the final 10 miles to its end at the White River Trailhead, also called the Indian Creek Trailhead, at 2,300 ft. what_to_bring: Ice axe (and microspikes/light crampons for early-season snow on the upper mountain)
Map/compass or GPS track — the route above the Indian Creek Trail is unmarked and route-finding heavy
Sturdy brush-worthy clothing/gaiters for the bushwhack to Airplane Lake

Of the three lines off Airplane Lake, the direct east-face route on slabby granite is generally cleaner than the brushier/loose talus variations
Expect a full, long day: budget 10-12+ hours car-to-car

backups.pro_needs: None — Southeast Slopes is a class 3 scramble typically climbed unroped; a rope and rack are not standard gear for this route.
backups.best_season: Late July through September is the reliable window; a first-hand July ascent found snow cover starting around 4,000 ft and continuous snow from about 4,700 ft, so early-season climbers should expect a snow climb on the upper east face/slopes and carry an ice axe. Snow returns by mid-to-late October at this elevation.
backups.approach: Drive to the White River Trailhead (also called the Indian Creek Trailhead) at the end of White River Road/FS-6400: from Leavenworth take US-2 west 15 miles to Coles Corner, turn onto SR-207 (Lake Wenatchee Highway) for 10.5 miles, then continue on White River Road/FS-6400 for a final 10 miles to the trailhead (2,300 ft). Follow the Indian Creek Trail north/west, crossing the White River and Indian Creek bridge, for roughly 4.5 miles. Near Airplane Creek, leave the maintained trail and bushwhack/scramble about 2,000 ft up to Airplane Lake (this leg runs 1.5-2 miles); from the lake, continue off-trail to the upper east slopes and summit via one of the three route options. Round trip is roughly 16 miles with about 5,300 ft of gain; a logged first-hand ascent recorded closer to 12 miles and 5,000 ft via a more direct Airplane Creek line, taking about 7.3 hours up and 4.4 hours down. From Airplane Lake, three lines reach the summit: the northeast ridge (working around a hidden, non-obvious cliff band north of the lake), a direct ascent of the clean upper east face slabs, or a looser steep-talus variation. Favoring the drainage about a quarter-mile downstream of Airplane Creek reportedly avoids the worst of the brush on the bushwhack in.
backups.descent_text: Most parties descend the same way they went up. At least one party notes an alternate ridge-descent option off the summit as an alternative to retracing the ascent line; whichever way is chosen, time creek crossings on Indian Creek/the White River for morning (lower, easier water) rather than late afternoon, when snowmelt runoff makes fords more difficult.
backups.bail: Descend the ascent slopes toward the approach drainage.

itinerary.cal: Snow commonly lingers on the upper east slope into July, so many parties carry an ice axe for the final scramble/snow section above ~4,700 ft.

days.note: From the White River trailhead, follow the flat Indian Creek Trail for 4.5 easy miles, then turn off onto a steep, brushy climber's path that gains 2,200 ft in 1.5 miles through old burn and vine maple to reach Airplane Lake. Camp on the lake's north-side peninsula, a known flat, bug-free spot used by most parties.

days.note: From camp, boulder-hop the lake's outlet and beeline toward the low point on the ridge east of the summit, then follow the ridge crest through a short rock band to the broad summit (register sits ~15 ft below and west of the high point). Early-season parties often kick steps up a continuous snowfield above ~4,700 ft. After descending to camp, break down and hike the full 6 miles back out to the trailhead the same day.

approach_variants.name: Indian Creek Trail and the Airplane Creek bushwhack to Airplane Lake
approach_variants.notes: From the road-end trailhead above Lake Wenatchee, the Indian Creek Trail crosses the White River on a footbridge — which has washed out in past years, forcing a ford — and runs up the valley through old growth and sections of burned, dead forest. Somewhere near Airplane Creek you leave the maintained tread; nothing marks the departure and it is easy to lose in brush or fog. The bushwhack from there to the lake is the hard part of the day: roughly two thousand feet of gain through devil's club, vine maple and blowdown, made worse by the standing dead timber. Favouring the drainage about a quarter mile downstream of Airplane Creek reportedly avoids the worst of the brush. Snow cover typically begins around 4,000 ft and becomes continuous near 4,700 ft in early season, so step-kicking on firm snow is normal here into July. Airplane Lake is the last reliable water and the only sensible flat camp. Time the White River and Indian Creek crossings for the morning, when the water is lower.
approach_variants.season: Late July through September is the reliable window. In July expect snow from around 4,000 ft and continuous cover above 4,700 ft, which makes the upper slopes a snow climb and calls for an axe.
hazards: off-trail bushwhacking through devil's club, vine maple and blowdown, worsened by burned standing timber
White River and Indian Creek crossings that get harder through the afternoon as snowmelt rises
hidden cliff bands north of Airplane Lake that can cliff out a party working toward the northeast ridge
lingering snow on the upper east slopes into July
loose rock and steep talus on some summit variations
a sheer northwest face that is not a descent or a bail option
approach_variants.baseFinding: GO EAST-FACING AND CLEAN, NOT NORTH AND BROKEN. From Airplane Lake the summit push starts at the foot of the upper east face at roughly 6,200 ft, where three distinct lines diverge and you have to pick one. The one to aim for is the direct ascent of the clean upper east-face slabs — recognisable because the rock is continuous and relatively clean rather than piled and broken, and because it faces the morning sun squarely. The other two are a steep, looser talus variation and the northeast ridge. The northeast ridge is the one to be careful of, and it carries its own negative marker: gaining it means working around a cliff band north of the lake that is not visible until you are on it and that has cliffed parties out. So if you find yourself traversing north of the lake into broken ground and then meeting a wall you did not expect, you are on the northeast-ridge variation, not the direct line. Snow coverage should decide the choice; on a snowy year the direct slabs may be a snow climb wanting an axe. The summit itself is broad with jagged rocks at the top, and the register sits west of the highest point among rocks about fifteen feet below it — worth knowing, because the true high point is not where the register is.

bivy.name: Airplane Lake
bivy.notes: This is the camp for Mount Saul and effectively the only one, and camping here is what turns a brutal outing into a reasonable two days. Done in a single push from the road the standard route runs about sixteen miles round trip with five thousand three hundred feet of gain, which is a long day by any measure and a very long one on ground this rough. The lake sits roughly two thousand two hundred feet above Indian Creek, in a large depression under the upper east slopes, with the summit still some two thousand feet above it — so a party sleeping here has the worst of the climbing behind them and a clean morning on the east slope and east face. THE APPROACH PATH IS THE HARD PART. It leaves the Indian Creek trail at about four and a half miles, immediately before a valley campsite, marked only by a sign stating that marking of routes is prohibited; there is no other signage and the track is faint. It climbs steeply through the 2016 burn, which means loose footing, no shade, blowdown that changes with every windstorm and standing dead timber overhead. Recent volunteer work has had the trail in good condition in places, but that is a season-by-season matter rather than a promise. Season is roughly mid-July into early October; the east side melts out reasonably early but the upper slopes hold snow and an axe is worth carrying in the first half of the summer.
bivy.water: The lake, and it is dependable through the climbing season along with snowmelt into the inlet early on. This is the last certain water on the mountain: the two thousand feet of slope between the lake and the summit carry nothing once the snow has gone. Fill everything here for the climb and for the night, and treat it.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness. A free self-issue permit is filled out at the White River trailhead register — no quota, no reservation, nothing to book. Party size is capped at twelve counting people and stock. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass covers parking at the trailhead. Camp back from the shoreline on existing bare ground; the basin is small. Carry a stove — the district runs summer fire restrictions on this dry east side as a matter of course and they are often total bans.
bivy.capacity: Informal ground on benches around the lake for one or two parties. Nothing developed, nothing signed, no toilet — and almost certainly nobody else there. This is a genuinely lightly visited basin and solitude is the main thing it offers.

bivy.name: White River road end trailhead
bivy.notes: The staging point for the whole trip, and worth its own entry because the drive is where this approach most often fails. The White River road leaves the Lake Wenatchee end and turns to gravel several miles before the trailhead, ending at about 2,300 feet where the White River trail, the Indian Creek trail, the Mount David trail and the Boulder Creek trail all begin. Getting the right one matters: only Indian Creek leads to Mount Saul. There are small developed forest campgrounds spaced along the road below the trailhead which are a better place to spend a night than the parking area itself if they are open, but they are primitive, first come and first served, and carry no potable supply. THE ROAD IS THE FRAGILE PART, AND IT IS CLOSED RIGHT NOW. Okanogan-Wenatchee closure order 06-17-07-2026-40 (Little Giant Fire), effective 3 September 2026 through 31 October 2026 unless rescinded sooner, closes FSR 6400 to the end of the road and lists the White River Trailhead. It is not named in the Wenatchee River District storm-damage road order (06-17-07-2026-11, 20 May 2026 through 31 December 2027), which closes seventeen other roads. When the road is shut low, the trailhead is a substantial road walk or bike ride further on and the trip changes character completely.
bivy.water: The White River is at the trailhead and needs treating. There is no potable supply and no tap. Fill here, and fill again from Indian Creek on the way up, because everything above the valley is dry.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park. The free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit comes from the register here rather than being arranged in advance — no quota, no reservation. Twelve-person party limit. Fire restrictions on this side are near-permanent through summer and commonly ban open flame entirely.
bivy.capacity: A gravel parking area at the road end with room to sleep in a vehicle, and no campground facilities. This is a roadhead recorded because a party arriving from the west side in the evening needs somewhere to be before starting an approach this long.

bivy.name: The Indian Creek valley camps and the Airplane Lake junction site
bivy.notes: The junction camp is the useful one and it is the landmark as much as the site: the climbers' path for Airplane Lake turns off immediately before it, so a party that reaches an obvious valley campsite and has seen no turning has just walked past the only one there is. Sleeping here rather than at the lake trades a shorter, easier first day for a much harder second one, and most parties would rather push to the lake. Where it earns its place is on the way out, and for a party that has been slowed by the road or the burn and does not want to start the two-thousand-foot climbers' path in the evening. The valley trail itself runs about ten and a half miles in total to the Pacific Crest Trail at Indian Pass, crossing the White River on a bridge right at the trailhead and then climbing very gently; it is brushy and boggy in places, which is a nuisance rather than an obstacle. Expect burn for long stretches, and treat the dead timber overhead as a real reason not to pitch under it in wind.
bivy.water: Indian Creek runs beside the trail for the whole of this stretch and water is abundant; parts of the valley trail are boggy in early season for the same reason. Every one of these sites has water at it into the autumn. This is the generous half of the approach and it ends the moment you start climbing.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the White River trailhead register, twelve-person limit, Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park. Fires are legal in existing rings at this elevation outside a burn ban, but bans are usual here from midsummer and much of the surrounding forest is fire-killed, so use a stove.
bivy.capacity: Scattered informal sites along the Indian Creek trail, one or two tents each, including the established spot immediately past the unsigned turn for Airplane Lake. Nothing developed and no facilities.

bivy.name: The east slope above Airplane Lake — no established camp
bivy.notes: The honest answer for this peak is that Airplane Lake is the camp and there is nothing above it worth having. The lake already puts the summit within a straightforward morning on the east slope and east face, so climbing higher with a pack buys almost nothing and costs the water, the shelter and the flat ground all at once. The northwest face is sheer and is not the way anyone goes; the east side is open scrambling terrain and the difficulty of this mountain lies in the approach rather than in the climbing. Where a high bivouac has any argument at all is for a party linking Saul with the ridge country toward Indian Head and the crest, which is a different and much longer trip, and even then the sensible pattern is to sleep at water and move over the tops in the day. Treat anything above the lake as emergency ground.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only, and only early in the season. From roughly August onward there is nothing at all above the lake, and anyone sleeping here carries every drop up two thousand feet. This is the mistake to avoid rather than a plan to make.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, twelve-person limit, Northwest Forest Pass at the White River trailhead. No fires at this elevation and nothing to burn. The ground is thin alpine turf and scree that scars for years — camp on rock or gravel if you camp at all.
bivy.capacity: None established. There is broken ground and the occasional flat spot on the slope between the lake and the summit rocks where a small party could put a tent down, but nothing has been built and nobody camps here as a matter of course. Recorded so the absence is stated rather than filled in with an invented site.

backups.overview: Old Guard Peak rises near Le Conte Mountain and Sentinel Peak along the southern half of the Ptarmigan Traverse, just south of Cache Col in Glacier Peak Wilderness, overlooking the Le Conte and South Cascade Glaciers. A precision differential-GPS survey puts it at 8,260 ft, a few feet above neighboring Sentinel Peak, and its prominence makes it a worthy detour for traverse parties.
backups.beta: Old Guard is usually tagged as a side-trip from a Ptarmigan Traverse camp near the Le Conte-Sentinel col (roughly 7,300-7,400 ft). From the col, rope up and cross the Le Conte Glacier, skirting crevasses and a bergschrund, to reach a snow ramp on the peak's northwest side. Above the ramp the route eases into a straightforward but somewhat loose, indistinct class 2-3 rock scramble to the summit. Most parties climb neighboring Sentinel Peak from the same camp in the same outing.
backups.turnaround: Because the route requires a roped glacier crossing exposed to afternoon sun on the Le Conte Glacier, start early enough to complete the glacier crossing while the snow is still firm, and set a turnaround that gets you back across the glacier before it softens into wet, crevasse-obscuring snow later in the day.
backups.face: West/northwest side, directly off the LeConte Glacier
backups.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the trailhead; no quota. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass on a vehicle left at the Downey Creek Trailhead.
backups.comms: No cell coverage anywhere along the LeConte Glacier, the Old Guard–Sentinel col, or the Ptarmigan Traverse corridor generally; carry a satellite messenger (inReach/SPOT) for emergency communication.
backups.descent: Reverse the west-side route back to the Le Conte Glacier

waypoints.name: Cascade Pass Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of Cascade River Road, 23.1 mi from Marblemount; NPS backcountry permit required for overnight stays, self-issue day-use is free.
waypoints.directions: Drive Cascade River Road east from Marblemount roughly 23 miles to its end at the Cascade Pass Trailhead at 3,660 ft — paved for about the first 10 miles, then good gravel the rest of the way. Check the road first: in some seasons, including 2026, vehicles are stopped at the Eldorado gate at mile 20 and the last 3 miles and 1,500 ft to the trailhead must be walked or biked. There is a parking area and a vault toilet at the road end. Day use is free and self-issue; a North Cascades backcountry permit is required for overnight camps, released seasonally through recreation.gov, and the camps along this traverse fill fast in peak season. Because the traverse exits at a different trailhead on the Suiattle River Road, most parties pre-arrange a car shuttle rather than leaving a vehicle here.

waypoints.name: Cascade Pass
waypoints.note: Trail tread ends at the pass; leave the maintained trail here and head south/southeast onto the Ptarmigan Traverse cross-country route.
waypoints.directions: The trail switchbacks around thirty times up a forested rib, gaining roughly 1,400 ft in the first two miles, then eases into a long ascending traverse through meadow and talus to the pass. Figure two and a half to three and a half hours. Snowfields can lie across the traverse well into summer.

waypoints.name: Cache Col
waypoints.note: Gap between Magic Mountain and Mix-up Peak at the head of Cache Glacier; gain it via a steep snow/scree gully, the crux route-finding point of day one.
waypoints.directions: Leave the trail at the pass and head south and east, traversing and climbing across the Mixup arm on boot path, talus and snow bands. Gain the shoulder, follow the snow ramp up, then drop onto the Cache Glacier and walk it to the col at its head. The step onto the glacier is short but steep and can be corniced, and an axe and crampons are normal here into midsummer.

waypoints.name: Kool-Aid Lake
waypoints.note: Small tarn on a bench south of Cache Col, the standard first-night bivy/base camp for the traverse; exposed, fog often wafts up from the valley below.
waypoints.directions: Descend the far side of the col — a steep snowfield that usually needs an axe and crampons well into midsummer — and lose several hundred feet to the bench holding the tarn. The runout below the snow is rocky, so this is not a place to glissade blind into fog.

waypoints.name: Red Ledge
waypoints.note: Narrow, exposed rock ledge cutting west from Art's Knoll that bypasses cliffs south of Kool-Aid Lake; can hold an open moat, verglas, or fresh snow that makes the traverse 'spicy' even in summer.
waypoints.directions: Climb out of the lake basin and traverse toward the cliff band running west off Art's Knoll, which from below looks like it stops the route entirely. Getting established usually means scrambling through the moat at the snow-rock margin and up a few feet of Class 3 to reach the ledge. Once on it the ledge is broad and walkable, unless it is holding snow or verglas.

waypoints.name: LeConte Glacier
waypoints.note: Broad glacier basin below Old Guard and Sentinel Peaks; rope up here and cross to the base of Old Guard's west/northwest side, watching for late-season crevasses near the peak's flanks.
waypoints.directions: This leg is far longer than the mileage on file suggests. Past the ledge the traverse crosses the Middle Cascade Glacier, climbs to the Spider-Formidable col and drops to the Yang Yang Lakes basin, after which the ledge system known as the goat path leads up onto the LeConte snowfield and glacier. It is a full day or more of committing glaciated terrain, travelled roped and with crevasse-rescue gear, not a short hop from the Red Ledge.

waypoints.name: Snowfinger / Couloir Base
waypoints.note: Steep snow couloir (Class 2/3) rising off the glacier to the base of the summit rock; firm early-morning snow can require an axe and crampons, softening to punchy postholing by afternoon.
waypoints.directions: From the glacier work to the foot of the snow finger rising toward the summit rock and get onto it wherever the moat or bergschrund allows — that transition is often the awkward move of the day. It is a few hundred feet of steep snow, best taken early while it is firm, since by afternoon it softens to punchy postholing and the runout is back onto the glacier.

waypoints.name: Old Guard Peak
waypoints.note: Short Class 3 scramble up grippy gabbro from the top of the couloir gains the true summit, with views across the LeConte Glacier to Sentinel Peak and Dome Peak.
waypoints.directions: Top out of the couloir and finish on a short Class 3 scramble up blocky gabbro, a few hundred feet on rock that takes hands but stays straightforward. Stash axe and crampons somewhere you will find them again, because the descent reverses this same couloir.

backups.detailed_rack: Standard glacier-travel kit: ice axe, crampons, a rope per team, pickets or ice screws, and a full crevasse-rescue kit (prusiks, pulley, mechanical ascenders), plus a helmet for the scramble above the col. No technical rock rack is used on this class 2-3 route.
pro_tips: Climb as part of the Ptarmigan Traverse
Pair with Sentinel and Le Conte
A harder 2-3 pitch low-5th-class alternative exists on the east side for parties wanting more technical climbing than the standard snow couloir line.
backups.pro_needs: None beyond glacier-travel protection - pickets/screws for crevasse rescue and a belay on the snow ramp if desired; the summit scramble itself is unroped class 2-3.
backups.best_season: Mid-July through August is most reliable, once the Ptarmigan Traverse itself is in season; the route depends on the whole traverse being passable, not just local conditions on Old Guard. Early season trips face larger cornices at Cache Col and a more consequential Red Ledge crux; a low-snow September can still work but exposes more bare glacier ice/crevasses on the LeConte Glacier crossing.
backups.approach: Drive Cascade River Road east from Marblemount roughly 23 miles (paved for about the first 10, then good gravel) to its end at the Cascade Pass Trailhead (3,660 ft; parking area and vault toilet, North Cascades NP wilderness permit required for overnight camps). In some seasons, including 2026, the road is gated to vehicles at Eldorado (mile 20), leaving the last 3 miles to the trailhead on foot or bike. From the trailhead, follow the Cascade Pass Trail, which switchbacks about 30 times up a forested rib, gaining roughly 1,400 ft in the first 2 miles before the grade eases into a long ascending traverse through meadows, talus, and lingering snowfields to Cascade Pass (5,400 ft) at about 3.7 miles — figure 2.5-3.5 hours to the pass. This is only the start: Old Guard Peak sits deep in the Ptarmigan Mountains and is normally reached via the classic Ptarmigan Traverse, not as a day trip from the pass. From Cascade Pass, leave the maintained trail and climb south and east on a boot path/talus toward Cache Col (~6,900 ft), a rocky saddle roughly 3 hours above the pass; a steep snowfield on the col's far side (often needing an axe and crampons through midsummer) descends to Kool-Aid Lake basin (~6,320-6,800 ft), a common first camp about 6-8 miles and 2,800 ft of gain from the trailhead. From Kool-Aid Lake the route crosses a band of steep snow (pickets useful) to reach the Red Ledge, an exposed but broad Class 3 rock traverse that is the traverse's first real crux, especially if snow-covered. Beyond the ledges, follow the true-left (climber's left) edge of the Middle Cascade Glacier, roping up for crevasse hazard, staying on the less-broken upper glacier, then continue to the Spider-Formidable Col (a whiteout-prone spot where altimeter/compass/GPS route-finding matters). From the col, descend steep snow and a long sidehill traverse over snow and rock down to Yang Yang Lakes, then continue via LeConte Pass and Sentinel Pass to White Rock Lakes/the LeConte Glacier area — the standard second or third camp, roughly 12-14 hours of cumulative travel from the trailhead for parties moving efficiently. Old Guard Peak is climbed from Sentinel Pass: contour onto the LeConte Glacier and ascend a moderate, gradually-angled snow couloir/snowfinger on the peak's northwest side (watch for a bergschrund/moat late season) to gain the summit ridge, then finish on short, low-Class-3 scrambling on solid, high-friction gabbro to the true summit (8,240-8,260 ft). Water is available at Kool-Aid Lake, Yang Yang Lakes, and White Rock Lakes/tarns near the LeConte Glacier; carry a full topo map and glacier gear, as this is committing, remote glacier terrain with no easy bail once past Cache Col.
backups.descent_text: Reverse the snow couloir and scramble down to the Le Conte-Sentinel col camp.
backups.bail: Retreat off the peak itself is straightforward (reverse to the Le Conte Glacier), but as of 2026 exiting the broader Ptarmigan Traverse is constrained: the Suiattle River Road washout closure has cut off vehicle access to the Downey Creek trailhead, so plan retreat via Cascade Pass instead.

pitch_detail.notes: Roped crossing of the Le Conte Glacier from the Le Conte-Sentinel col, skirting crevasses and a bergschrund to reach the base of Old Guard's northwest snow ramp.
Snow couloir/ramp gains a short, somewhat loose rock scramble (class 2-3) to the summit.

climate.fall: Early-season storms can drop new snow on the high traverse terrain and complicate glacier travel and route-finding.
climate.summer: Best weather window for the traverse, but afternoon thunderstorms and lingering snow on the glaciers are still possible into July.
climate.winter: Not a winter/spring objective — deep snow, avalanche hazard, and unplowed access roads make the approach impractical.
climate.typical: Cool, changeable high-alpine conditions typical of the North Cascades crest; mornings are usually firmer for glacier travel, with afternoon cloud buildup and a real chance of thunderstorms or sudden weather shifts common along the Ptarmigan Traverse.

bySeason.fall: September can still work in low-snow years with more exposed glacier ice/crevasses and colder overnight temps; shortening daylight is a factor on the long traverse approach.
bySeason.spring: Generally too much unstable snow on Cache Col and the Red Ledge crux; road may still be gated at Eldorado.
bySeason.summer: July-August is the core season once the Ptarmigan Traverse route itself is passable; snow bridges and cornices at Cache Col are more consolidated by mid-to-late July.
bySeason.winter: Not a winter objective - Cascade River Road is snowed in and the approach is avalanche terrain.

emergency.notes: Remote Ptarmigan Traverse terrain in Glacier Peak Wilderness (not North Cascades National Park - the park boundary is at Cache Col, north of here); self-sufficiency essential. approach_variants.name: Cascade Pass and the traverse corridor to the LeConte Glacier
approach_variants.notes: This is a side trip off a multi-day high traverse, not a day climb. From the Cascade Pass Trailhead at the end of the Cascade River Road, the maintained trail switchbacks up a forested rib and eases into a long ascending traverse through meadow and talus to the pass, where the tread ends. Leave the trail there and head south and east, traversing and climbing across the Mixup arm on boot path, talus and snow bands, then onto the Cache Glacier and up it to Cache Col; the step onto the glacier is short but steep and can be corniced, and an axe and crampons are normal here into midsummer. Descend the steep snowfield on the far side to the bench holding Kool-Aid Lake, the usual first camp. From there the Red Ledge bypasses the cliff band west of the knoll above, entered by scrambling through the moat at the snow-rock margin. Past the ledge, the corridor crosses the Middle Cascade Glacier, climbs to the Spider-Formidable col and drops to the Yang Yang Lakes basin, after which a ledge system leads up onto the LeConte snowfield and glacier. Camp near the col between LeConte and Sentinel, or at White Rock Lakes, and climb the peak from there.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July through August is most reliable, since the route depends on the whole corridor being passable rather than on local conditions. Early trips face larger cornices at Cache Col and a more consequential Red Ledge; a low-snow autumn exposes more bare glacier ice.
hazards: roped glacier travel with crevasses on the LeConte Glacier, and a bergschrund or moat at the foot of the snow ramp late season
loose rock on the upper scramble
remoteness with no easy bail once past Cache Col
steep early-season snow on the col approaches and on the ramp itself
the ramp softens to punchy postholing by afternoon, with the runout back onto the glacier
approach_variants.baseFinding: ONE SNOW RAMP RISES OFF THE GLACIER TO THE SUMMIT RIDGE, AND THE MOAT AT ITS FOOT IS THE GATE. From the LeConte Glacier the peak shows a single moderate, gradually-angled snow finger running up to the summit rocks; that ramp is the route, and getting onto it — finding the spot where the moat or bergschrund at its base allows a step across — is usually the awkward move of the day. It is a few hundred feet of steep snow, best taken early while it is firm, because by afternoon it turns to punchy postholing and the runout is straight back onto the glacier. Above it, the finish is a short scramble of a few hundred feet on blocky, high-friction gabbro that takes hands and stays straightforward. Two negative markers. Sentinel Peak is the adjacent summit immediately WEST of this one and is a few feet lower than this one — if the peak you are under is the western of the pair, you are below Sentinel. And if the rock above the top of your snow ramp turns into two pitches of mid-fifth-class climbing rather than a hands-on scramble, you are on this peak's east ridge, which is a real route but not this one. Stash the axe and crampons somewhere you will find them; the descent reverses the same ramp.

bivy.name: Yang Yang Lakes
bivy.notes: The second camp for most north-to-south parties, sitting in a shallow bowl below Le Conte Mountain after the drop off the Middle Cascade Glacier. It is the natural base for Old Guard Peak, whose summit is reached from the Le Conte Glacier above by a class 2 to 3 snow couloir and short scramble on the west side, or by two to three pitches of easy to moderate fifth class on the east ridge. Sentinel Peak is the other objective from here and the two are usually taken together. The descent into and climb out of this basin is steep on both sides, so parties running late often push instead to Le Conte Pass above and accept the thinner water. Snow lingers in the bowl well into July, which is when the camping is easiest and the heather is protected.
bivy.water: Two lakes, which makes this the most dependable water on the northern half of the traverse. Nothing above it is reliable: the ridge camps toward Formidable and the ground up at Le Conte Pass are snowmelt-only late in the season, though the pass usually holds tarns into midsummer.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit at the trailhead register. Camp at least 100 feet back from the lakeshores. No campfires; the ground here is thin alpine heather that does not recover.
bivy.capacity: Several unimproved sites in the heather between the two small lakes, enough for two or three parties. No toilet and no established platforms.

bivy.name: Kool-Aid Lake
bivy.notes: The first camp on the traverse coming from Cascade Pass, reached by climbing to Cache Col and dropping a short but awkward distance southwest to the tarn. It is where the permit regime changes, which is the practical reason to know it exists even if you are only passing through. Published elevations vary by a couple of hundred feet, with figures around 6,300 the most common and one outlier several hundred feet higher, so treat the number as approximate rather than a waypoint. From here the day ahead crosses the Red Ledge and the Middle Cascade Glacier toward Old Guard Peak and Sentinel, and there are further ridge bivouacs at around 6,300 ft just past the Red Ledge if the lake is full or the hour is late. Early season this is a snow camp with easy water everywhere; late season it is bare heather and rock and the tarn is the only source.
bivy.water: The tarn itself plus snowmelt runnels feeding it. Reliable in July and through most of August, but it is a shallow pool with a small catchment and it can drop to a warm, silty puddle by September in a light snow year. Cache Col just above has no water at all, so parties camping high on the shoulder have to carry from here or melt snow.
bivy.permit: Once you cross Cache Col you are out of North Cascades National Park and into Glacier Peak Wilderness, so no park permit covers this camp. Sign the free self-issue wilderness register instead. If you spend a night on the park side, including at Cascade Pass or on the shoulder below the Cache Glacier, that night does need an NPS wilderness permit collected in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Campfires have no place at this elevation; carry a stove.
bivy.capacity: A handful of small heather and gravel platforms around a tiny tarn, comfortable for two or three parties and crowded beyond that. No facilities, no toilet, nothing built.

bivy.name: White Rock Lakes
bivy.notes: The third camp and the one most parties remember, reached from Yang Yang across the Le Conte Glacier and the Le Conte-Sentinel col, then down a long traverse under Sentinel and Old Guard. It looks straight across at Dome Peak and the Dana Glacier, which is the day that follows. Sinister Peak is not climbed from here directly, but this is the last camp with easy water before the ground gets serious: the Chickamin and Dome glaciers are the way to Sinister and to the Gunsight Range, and everything from here east is snow, ice and rock with no running water. It is a windy basin and the good sites are the sheltered ones near the outlet. Snow can cover the lakes into early July, which some parties prefer because it makes the camping flat and the water trivially available.
bivy.water: The lakes, fed by the snowfields and the Le Conte and Dana ice above them. Normally good all season, though the outlet stream can be reduced to a trickle late in a dry summer and the smaller pools go stagnant.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit. Keep camps 100 feet from the water. Stoves only.
bivy.capacity: Open benches near the outlet of the larger lake and scattered spots around the basin, wind-exposed but roomy enough for several parties. Unimproved, no toilet.

backups.name: Deep Blue
backups.fa: Completed 2020 as a multi-year project; Mike Kerzhner with Blake Herrington, Luke Stefurak, Matt Carroll, Jasna Hodzic and Liz Hadley contributing at different stages.
gear: rope long enough for the bolted rappel descent
hazards: Same approach hazards as Vanishing Point (steep brush/gully, fixed-line forested rib, loose rock).
High commitment/exposure on a remote alpine rock tower once established above the lower pitches.
backups.overview: A 12-pitch, fully-bolted 5.13c testpiece on Dolomite Tower's northeast face, starting about 100 ft left of Vanishing Point and climbing steep, technical rock through several roof systems to a 5.13 crux high on the wall.
backups.beta: Deep Blue begins on a fin-like flake right off the ground — mount the flake and pull a small bulge into easier climbing. Lower/mid pitches include an overhang leading into face climbing to a small ledge below a roof, a pitch through a roof with technical edges to a ledge, and a stretch of 5.11 climbing to a higher ledge below the crux. Higher up, steep 5.10+ lieback flakes lead to an alcove, then a roof with a bouldery V6 crux on perfect edges (~25m pitch), before steep, sequential climbing on good holds leads toward the 5.13c crux pitch itself (~35m, sustained overhanging climbing to a vertical-face crux) and a further 5.12 pitch (~35m) through another roof. The route was developed over several years and finished in 2020; it climbs in 12 pitches with link-up options for parties wanting to move faster, and multiple parties have completed it car-to-car in a day without simul-climbing.
backups.turnaround: As with Vanishing Point, the approach and descent both traverse exposed, technical terrain best done in daylight — plan a start early enough that the technical approach, all 12 pitches, and the rappel descent finish before dark.
backups.rappels: Rappel anchors on the tower and along the fixed-line approach sections were replaced with stainless steel during the 2020 work on this face and are spaced roughly 30-35 m apart, so the line can be rappelled with a 60 m rope; a 70 m allows a single-rappel reversal of part of the approach.

backups.detailed_rack: The technical pitches are fully bolted (essentially a big-wall sport route); a single BD cam set from #0.2 to #0.75 plus roughly 16 quickdraws (including 2-4 alpine draws for wandering pitches) covers the route. Cams are needed only on the roped approach pitches below the true start, not on the bolted climbing itself.

pro_tips: The route starts on a distinctive fin-like flake about 100 ft left of Vanishing Point's start — don't confuse the two lines at the base.

Multiple link-up options exist between pitches for parties wanting to move quickly; it has been done car-to-car in a day without simul-climbing.
watch_out: Sustained hard climbing starts essentially at the ground — there's no easy pitch to warm up on before things get technical.

backups.pro_needs: Almost entirely bolt-protected; the small cam rack exists mainly for the shared roped approach pitches rather than the route proper.
backups.best_season: Same window as Vanishing Point: roughly late June/July through September, once the approach gully has cleared of snow and running water; the shared NE aspect keeps the wall relatively cool/shaded through most of the day.
backups.approach: Identical to Vanishing Point's approach from the Barclay Lake Trailhead (see that route) — Barclay Creek Trail to the wash/gully system, fixed-line forested rib, and roped approach slabs to the base of the tower; Deep Blue's start is about 100 ft left of Vanishing Point's first pitch.
backups.descent_text: Because every anchor on Deep Blue is bolted, parties descend by rappelling the route itself rather than walking off; bring a rope long enough (and doubled rap tat/rings as needed) to link the bolted stations back to the ground.
backups.bail: Bolted anchors at every belay allow retreat by rappel from essentially any point on the route.

backups.overview: Massie Peak is a remote, seldom-visited summit on the ridge above Massie Lake in the Phelps Creek/Chiwawa River high country of the Glacier Peak Wilderness. It has no maintained trail to its summit and is usually climbed as a side-trip from longer backcountry loops through Buck Creek Pass, High Pass, Liberty Cap, and neighboring Chiwawa Mountain, reached via the unmaintained 'Massie Lake High Route' — an old sheepherder's path — rather than any signed trail.
backups.beta: From the Trinity/Buck Creek Trailhead, follow the Chiwawa River Trail north about 3 miles to the unsigned, unmaintained 'Massie Lake' way-trail (an old sheepherder driveway marked by axe/burn blazes on trees) and climb steeply to Massie Lake. From the lake, gain the ridge above and continue cross-country toward the summit, bypassing a false summit before reaching the true top. The line is difficult to follow, brushy, and has claimed parties onto unwanted 4th-class terrain when off-route; a Aug-2024 trip report logged 14.75 miles round trip, about 5,400' of gain, and 7 hours car-to-car via a non-standard east-ridge/south-ridge variant, noting the descent line is easy to lose.
backups.turnaround: Given the difficult, unmaintained approach and real risk of getting cliffed-out or losing the route in poor visibility or failing light, set a firm turnaround time based on your pace back to Massie Lake and the trailhead, and turn back if you have not located the lake or the ridge above it well before your planned midpoint.

backups.approach: From the Trinity Trailhead (~2,820 ft, at the end of Chiwawa River/Chiwawa Valley Road, Forest Road 6200, reached via Coles Corner and Hwy 207), pick up the Chiwawa River Trail #1550 and follow it upstream through forest for roughly 4 miles. Watch the left (west) side of the trail for an 'M' blazed/carved into a tree — this marks the unsigned, unmaintained sheepherder's path up to Massie Lake, and it's easy to walk past if you're not looking for it. Ford the Chiwawa River at this point (can run cold and pushy with snowmelt into early summer; trekking poles help, expect wet feet) and pick up the old sheep-drive trail, which climbs steeply via a mix of tree blazes and intermittent boot-track for about 3 miles and roughly 1,900-2,100 ft of gain to Massie Lake (~6,600-6,700 ft), a clear trout-holding tarn with a couple of established campsites. There is essentially no reliable water between the river ford and the lake, so fill up at the Chiwawa. From Massie Lake, continue on the faint sheep/game-trail tread of the Massie Lake High Route, contouring northwest roughly 1.5 miles toward Pass No Pass, then leave that trail and turn uphill (climber's right) onto Massie Peak's broad west ridge. Follow the ridge crest east for a bit over a mile — talus and heather with a few short rock steps, generally Class 2 with brief Class 3 moves near the summit block — to the 7,533 ft summit. The main hazard throughout is route-finding: the sheepherder path disappears in places, blazes thin out above treeline, and the entire line beyond the Chiwawa River Trail is off-trail, unsigned, and easy to lose in flat light — bring a map/GPS track. Snow and ice can linger on shaded sections of the high route and ridge well into summer; many parties carry microspikes and a light ice axe for trips before mid-July.
backups.descent_text: Reverse the ascent line: downclimb the west ridge (Class 2-3, some loose rock underfoot) back to the point where you gained it from the Massie Lake High Route, rejoin that faint tread and follow it back southeast to Massie Lake, then descend the steep sheepherder path back down to the Chiwawa River ford and out the Chiwawa River Trail #1550 to Trinity Trailhead. This is a walk-off/downclimb with no rappelling anywhere on the route — there are no fixed anchors reported on Massie Peak's west ridge or the approach gully, consistent with its Class 2-3 scrambling character. The trickiest part of the descent is simply staying on the correct (badly faded) line: the sheep trail is easy to lose both up in the high-route traverse and on the steep drop back to the river, and a mistaken line can dead-end in cliff bands or brush. Some parties instead continue past Massie Lake and pick a 'route of least resistance' down open slopes directly to Buck Creek Trail when linking Massie Peak with neighboring summits (Mount Cleator, Helmet Butte, Liberty Cap) on a multi-day loop, but for a straightforward out-and-back on the West Route, reversing the ascent line described above is the standard descent.
backups.bail: Retreat by reversing the ascent line back toward Massie Lake and down to the Chiwawa River crossing, then out the Chiwawa River Trail to Trinity Trailhead. No technical rope work is typically required to bail, but parties who wander off the standard line have encountered short 4th-class cliff bands that require careful, deliberate downclimbing.

approach_variants.name: Chiwawa River Trail to the sheepherder's path and Massie Lake
approach_variants.notes: From the road-end trailhead at the top of the Chiwawa valley, fill out the free self-issue wilderness permit and follow the Chiwawa River Trail #1550 upstream through forest, watching the west side of the tread for the marker described below. Ford the river at that point — it can run thigh-deep and swift with early-season snowmelt, so cross in the morning when flows are lowest — and pick up the old sheep-drive path, which climbs steeply on a mix of axe and burn blazes and intermittent boot track to Massie Lake. There is essentially no reliable water between the ford and the lake. From the lake the faint sheep and game tread of the high route contours northwest toward the pass ahead; leave it and turn uphill onto the peak's broad west ridge.

approach_variants.baseFinding: TWO THINGS FACING EACH OTHER ACROSS THE TRAIL MARK IT: A LARGE BOULDER JUTTING IN FROM THE EAST, AND AN 'M' WITH AN ARROW CARVED INTO A TREE ON THE WEST. The boulder is what you actually see first. There is no sign and no trail number, and the path it marks is an old sheep-drive route that is easy to walk straight past. The river is forded immediately below the junction, with piled driftwood the only help across, so the ford and the carved letter go together. The serious trap here is a decoy: a false set of markers — a boulder in the bank and logs and arrows suggesting the lake — has existed roughly a mile short of the real junction, and a party that took it spent hours bushwhacking up the wrong hillside and came out on the ridge high above the lake. So do not settle for arrows alone; you want the boulder and the carved 'M' opposite one another, and cairns have since been built on both sides of the trail at the true crossing. Above the ford a steep, poorly-marked boot track climbs to the lake on axe and burn blazes that thin out with height. From the lake the faint high route contours away; leave it and turn uphill onto the broad west ridge, the only named feature near that decision being a shoulder around 6,420 ft.

climbing_route.label: Broad west ridge to the summit
climbing_route.notes: Leave the Massie Lake High Route short of Pass No Pass and turn uphill (climber's right) onto Massie Peak's broad west ridge, then follow the ridge crest east for a bit over a mile to the 7,533 ft summit — talus and heather with a few short rock steps, generally Class 2 with brief Class 3 moves near the summit block. Route-finding is the main hazard: blazes thin out above treeline and the line is unsigned and easy to lose in flat light, so carry a map/GPS track. Snow and ice linger on shaded sections of the ridge well into summer; many parties carry microspikes and a light ice axe before mid-July.

bivy.name: Massie Lake basin
bivy.notes: This is the climbing camp for Massie Peak and effectively the only one, because everything above it is dry and everything below it is a long way down. From the Trinity trailhead the Buck Creek trail runs a mile and a half to the junction, the Chiwawa River trail carries on up the valley and crosses the river on a bridge, and about three miles along it the Massie Lake trail turns off and climbs roughly two miles and fifteen hundred feet to the lake. THAT LAST STRETCH IS THE DIFFICULTY AND IT IS NOT A TRAIL IN ANY USEFUL SENSE. It is an unsigned and unmaintained old sheep driveway, steep, brushy and lost altogether in places, and the standard complaint about this lake is the amount of bushwhacking involved in reaching it. Expect to lose the line more than once and to be pushing through vegetation on the steepest part of the day. From camp the west route on Massie Peak goes on open slopes above the basin and is a scramble rather than a climb. The reward for the thrash is genuine solitude and good fishing; the register-level traffic here is a fraction of what the Buck Creek Pass side sees. Season is roughly mid-July into early October, later than a lake this height would suggest because the brush is at its worst when it is wet.
bivy.water: The lake, and it is dependable all season. This is the last certain water on the climb and the reason to camp here rather than higher: the slopes and benches above the basin run on snowmelt only and are dry by August in an ordinary year. Fill completely before going up. Treat it, though the shoreline sees very little use.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness. A free self-issue permit is filled out at the Trinity trailhead register — no quota, no reservation, nothing to book in advance. Party size is capped at twelve counting people and stock together. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass covers parking at Trinity. Camp back from the shoreline and on existing bare ground; this is a small basin and it marks easily. Carry a stove — summer fire restrictions on this dry east side are routine and often total.
bivy.capacity: Informal ground around the lake for one or two parties. There is nothing developed, nothing signed and no toilet, and the basin is small — but it is also so little visited that competition for space is not a realistic worry.

bivy.name: Trinity trailhead roadhead
bivy.notes: The staging point, and it is recorded because the drive is the part of this trip that most often goes wrong. In a normal year the Chiwawa River road runs about twenty-two miles from the Lake Wenatchee end, with the last stretch rough gravel genuinely unsuited to low clearance, and arriving at the end of it late and tired is how parties end up starting the walk in badly. From the roadhead a short section of closed road leads onto the Buck Creek trail, and the junction where the Chiwawa River trail branches right for Massie is a mile and a half in. THE ROAD IS SHUT ABOVE ATKINSON FLAT under a storm-damage order running into 2027, with the 2026 fire closure sitting over the same corridor on top of it, and while that stands there is no legal way to drive to this roadhead at all. When the road is open again, expect it to remain the fragile part of any plan here: it has been damaged repeatedly, it carries no through traffic to justify quick repair, and the trailhead is far enough up it that a single washout removes the whole approach.
bivy.water: The Chiwawa River is close by and needs treating. There is no potable supply and no tap anywhere at this end of the road. Fill everything here, since the valley trail above is good for water and the climb to the lake is not.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park. The free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit is taken from the register here — no quota, no reservation. Twelve-person party limit including stock. Fire restrictions bite hard on this side from midsummer and commonly ban all open flame including in existing rings.
bivy.capacity: A gravel parking area at the end of the public road with room to sleep in a vehicle. It is a roadhead, not a campground — no fee site, no tables, no toilet you should count on. The developed campgrounds strung along the Chiwawa River road below it are the proper drive-in option and are recorded in the Entiat and Holden file rather than repeated here.

bivy.name: The Chiwawa River trail camps above the bridge
bivy.notes: These are the first-night camps for a party that has driven a long way, or the last-night camps for one walking out, and on this approach both cases are common. The river bridge where the Buck Creek trail crosses is the usual spot and is the obvious place to stop, being flat, sheltered and on good water. Camping here rather than pushing on matters because the Massie Lake turn is unsigned and the driveway above it is steep and vague — that is ground you want to meet in the morning with fresh legs and a full day, not at dusk. The valley walking below is gentle and fast, so a party that gets away from the road in the afternoon can be here comfortably. THE ROAD CLOSURE CHANGES THE ARITHMETIC ENTIRELY. With the Chiwawa River road shut above Atkinson Flat, Trinity is roughly eleven road miles further on, which turns the walk to these camps into a long day on its own or a bike shuttle, and turns the trip as a whole from two nights into three or four.
bivy.water: The Chiwawa River is alongside for this whole stretch and every one of these sites has water at it into the autumn. This is where the approach is generous with water, and it is worth knowing because the climb to Massie Lake is the steep, hot, brushy part and there is nothing dependable on it.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit from the Trinity trailhead register, twelve-person limit, Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park. Fires are legal below the high country in existing rings outside a burn ban, but the Chiwawa valley is dry and bans are the norm from midsummer, so plan on a stove.
bivy.capacity: Scattered informal sites in the timber along the valley floor, including good ground where the trail crosses the river on the bridge. One or two parties each, nothing developed, and rarely anyone else there.

bivy.name: The benches above Massie Lake — no established camp
bivy.notes: Recorded honestly: Massie Peak is a day objective from the lake and there is no practical reason to sleep higher. The scramble from the basin is short enough that the only argument for going up is to be on the crest at first light, and the cost is carrying water two thousand feet and sleeping exposed with nothing to shelter behind. The one situation where these benches genuinely earn their place is the traverse northwest on the old sheepherder's line toward Pass No Pass and the Buck Creek Pass country, which runs two and a half to three miles on faint stock and game tracks that come and go, and which a party will not finish in the same day they climb the peak. If you are doing that, sleeping high on the way out makes sense. If you are climbing Massie and walking back down the driveway, it does not. Either way, do not plan on finding water and do not plan on finding a flat, cleared spot.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only, and only early in the season. By August there is usually nothing at all above the lake, and a party sleeping up here is carrying every drop from the basin below. This is the single most common way to get the trip wrong.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, twelve-person limit, Northwest Forest Pass at Trinity. No fires this high — carry a stove. The ground is thin subalpine turf that holds a footprint for years, so pitch on gravel or rock and leave the meadow alone.
bivy.capacity: None established. There is open ground on the benches and in the meadows above the lake where a small party could put down a tent, but nothing has been built, nothing is marked, and nobody camps here as a matter of course. That is worth saying plainly rather than inventing a site.
